newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. offers Mexico $6 million for drug war.
newsitem.headline: U.S. offers Mexico $6 million for drug war.

text.p: The United States promised Mexico new funds on Monday to help fight drug smuggling as the two countries played down differences over the issues that threaten to cloud this week's visit by President Bill Clinton.

The State Department said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and her Mexican counterpart, Jose Angel Gurria, agreed to seek a way out of a dispute over whether U.S. drug enforcement agents can carry weapons in Mexico.

Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that in a meeting after an annual session of cabinet ministers from both countries, Albright told Gurria Washington would extend $6 million to Mexico to help train counter-narcotics agents.
New agents needed to be recruited to replace others fired in an anti-corruption purge by the Mexican government, Burns told reporters before Clinton arrived in Mexico City for a two-day visit.
He described the aid as "new money, immediately available", and said Gurria had gratefully accepted it. U.S. officials said it came from State Department contingency funds.

Burns reported no agreement on whether U.S. agents could bear arms in Mexico, one of several drug issues that have vexed Washington's ties with its southern neighbour. Mexico is the transit country for most of the cocaine reaching the United States.

Gurria repeated last week's refusal by Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo to permit this, but Burns said Gurria and Albright "agreed a way had to be found to ensure the safety of Americans" operating against drugs in Mexico.
"We have not agreed on specific ways to do that," Burns said. "But Gurria specifically said he wants the DEA (U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration) in Mexico and he wants them (agents) to be safe."

Albright earlier stressed at a news conference that drugs "have to be dealt with cooperatively," while Gurria, in a speech to a Bi-national Commission grouping U.S. and Mexican Cabinet members called for an end to cross-border frictions.

Mexico has criticised the White House's policy of "certifying," or publicly judging, the anti-drug efforts of countries around the world -- a policy sensitive in Mexico this year because its performance was criticised.
Albright, addressing the commission, applauded Mexico's measures to crack down on drugs and praised Zedillo as a "determined partner" in the anti-narcotics battle.

She praised steps to stamp out money laundering and ease extradition of traffickers. But, she said, "we must follow up on last year's high narcotics seizure rates by intensifying joint operations and putting major traffickers behind bars."

Underscoring continued doubts in Washington about Mexican drug policy, U.S. Senator Phil Gramm on Monday urged Clinton to raise in Mexico the case of convicted drug trafficker Rafael Caro Quintero, who last month won an appeal in a Mexican court against his sentence for the 1985 killing of American drug enforcement agent Enrique Camarena.

He said the decision, "coming amid the mounting evidence of drug corruption in Mexico, is not reassuring to anyone concerned about justice for Agent Camerena's killers or about the river of drugs and death that continues to flow from Mexico into Texas."
